passages.t: A house built by wisdom, and those led away to death
passages.happening:
‘Do not envy wicked men or desire their company’ (verse 1), for their hearts plan violence (verse 2).

“By wisdom a house is built and by understanding it is established; through knowledge its rooms are filled with every precious and beautiful treasure” (verses 3-4). ‘A wise man is strong’ (verse 5), and wars are won with good counsel (verse 6).

‘If you faint in the day of distress, how small is your strength’ (verse 10). Then a command: ‘Rescue those being led away to death, and restrain those stumbling toward the slaughter’ (verse 11). If you say you did not know, ‘does not He who weighs hearts consider it?’ (verse 12). He will repay each person according to what they have done.

‘Eat honey, my son, for it is good’ (verse 13). ‘Know therefore that wisdom is sweet to your soul. If you find it, there is a future for you, and your hope will never be cut off’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
This chapter ends the Words of the Wise (22:17 to 24:22) and adds a short appendix. Verses 3 and 4 are a small building poem: wisdom builds the house, understanding makes it firm, knowledge fills its rooms.

What is new here is the urgency of verses 10 to 12. The wise are not only told to avoid evil. They are told to act when someone else is in danger. And they are warned in advance about the easiest excuse, that they did not know. God weighs hearts, and he knows what was known.

Verse 10 is not a rebuke to anyone who is worn out. It is a call to find strength for the hard day, because the next verse asks the reader to help others in theirs.

As honey is sweet to the taste, so wisdom is sweet to the soul. Wisdom is not a grim duty. It is a good thing to taste.
passages.later: The psalm gives the same command: ‘Rescue the weak and needy; save them from the hand of the wicked’ (Psalm 82:4). And Isaiah speaks to the faint of verse 10: ‘But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength’ (Isaiah 40:31).
passages.asks: ‘We did not know’ is the easiest excuse. Ask whose danger you know about and have looked away from. And ask where you need strength for your own hard day, and where you could find it.

passages.t: Seven times down, and up again
passages.happening:
Do not lie in wait to harm the home of the righteous (verse 15), ‘For though a righteous man may fall seven times, he still gets up; but the wicked stumble in bad times’ (verse 16).

‘Do not gloat when your enemy falls, and do not let your heart rejoice when he stumbles’ (verse 17), or the LORD will see it, disapprove, and turn his anger from him (verse 18).

‘Do not fret over evildoers, and do not be envious of the wicked’ (verse 19), ‘For the evil man has no future’ (verse 20). ‘My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not associate with the rebellious’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Seven is a number of fullness. The righteous may be knocked down again and again and still not be finished, because God holds them up.

Verses 17 and 18 forbid gloating even over an enemy. The surprise is the reason: if you gloat, the LORD may turn his anger away from your enemy. Gloating is itself a sin he sees.

Verses 21 and 22 set loyalty to the king beside the fear of the LORD. They come from a monarchy where royal officials were trained in wisdom and rebellion was both a political and a moral danger.
passages.later: The psalm says of the righteous: ‘Though he falls, he will not be overwhelmed, for the LORD is holding his hand’ (Psalm 37:24). And the prophet Micah speaks for a people who fell: “Do not gloat over me, my enemy! Though I have fallen, I will arise; though I sit in darkness, the LORD will be my light” (Micah 7:8).
passages.hard:
Does verse 16 promise that good people always recover from disaster?

Verse 16 says that though a righteous man may fall seven times, he still gets up. It is easy to read this as a guarantee that the righteous always bounce back. But it is a proverb, and a proverb describes how life usually goes under God, not a promise for every case.

Seven is a number of fullness, so the verse is about endurance. The righteous are knocked down again and again, and they are not finished, because God upholds them.

Other parts of Scripture, especially Job, Ecclesiastes and the lament psalms, speak honestly of righteous people who suffer long and die without any visible recovery. Read together, the Bible holds both truths. God sustains his people, and his sustaining does not always look like restored fortunes in this life. No one should say to a person who has not recovered that they must not be righteous.
passages.asks: The righteous fall and get up again. Ask where you have been knocked down, and what it would mean to get up one more time with God's help. And ask whether there is anyone whose fall you have quietly enjoyed.

passages.t: Honest judges, no revenge, and the slacker's field
passages.happening:
A short new collection begins: ‘These also are sayings of the wise: To show partiality in judgment is not good’ (verse 23). Whoever tells the guilty they are innocent will be cursed by peoples, ‘but it will go well with those who convict the guilty’ (verse 25). ‘An honest answer given is like a kiss on the lips’ (verse 26).

‘Complete your outdoor work and prepare your field; after that, you may build your house’ (verse 27). Do not testify against your neighbor without cause (verse 28). And do not say you will pay someone back for what he did to you (verse 29).

Then the teacher tells what he saw. ‘I went past the field of a slacker and by the vineyard of a man lacking judgment’ (verse 30). Thorns and thistles covered it, and its stone wall had fallen. ‘I observed and took it to heart; I looked and received instruction’ (verse 32): ‘A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit’ (verses 33-34).
passages.hearers:
Verse 23 has its own heading, showing again that Proverbs was compiled from several sources by editors who marked the joins.

Justice was done at the town gate, where elders heard cases and witnesses spoke. Partiality, declaring the guilty innocent, and false testimony were the ways a town's justice was corrupted, and everyone depended on honest courts. An honest answer like a kiss on the lips was probably a sign of close friendship and loyalty.

Verse 29 faces the old instinct for payback. Feuds and retaliation were common, and Israel's law set limits on punishment, but the private urge to repay a wrong was strong. The wise refuse it, and leave repayment to God (verse 12).

The hill country of Judah was farmed in terraced fields and vineyards held in by stone walls. Left alone for a few seasons, a plot would be overgrown with thorns and its walls would slump and fall. The closing lines repeat 6:10-11 almost word for word. ‘A little’ is said three times, like the small, reasonable delays that add up to ruin.
passages.later: Paul says what verse 29 says: ‘Do not repay anyone evil for evil’ (Romans 12:17). And Job counted gloating as a sin he had refused: ‘If I have rejoiced in my enemy’s ruin’ (Job 31:29).
passages.asks: The slacker's ruin came from a little sleep, a little slumber. Ask which small delays are piling up in your life. And ask whether you are holding a grudge you mean to repay, and whether you could leave it with God.
